builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: ToolTurns: Benchmarking LLM Agents in Multi-Turn Dialogue
summary: This benchmark replaces single-turn tool-use evaluations with multi-turn dialogues that test clarification, tool use, and context retention. It requires implementing or adopting the open-source user simulator and checker--fixer pipeline, which adds evaluation complexity and compute overhead. The method can fail if the user simulator does not accurately reflect real user behavior or if the checker--fixer introduces biases in turn revision.
rationale: The reader should test this benchmark to evaluate multi-turn tool-use capabilities in production agents, as it provides a realistic assessment of dialogue performance but requires validation against specific workloads.

claims.statement: This benchmark replaces single-turn tool-use evaluations with multi-turn dialogues that test clarification, tool use, and context retention. It requires implementing or adopting the open-source user simulator and checker--fixer pipeline, which adds evaluation complexity and compute overhead. The method can fail if the user simulator does not accurately reflect real user behavior or if the checker--fixer introduces biases in turn revision.
The best agent resolves 69.6% of individual requests but completes only 39.8% of full dialogues, with every evaluated model scoring lower on follow-up requests than on the initial request.
